# Hours, Output and the Pilot Problem: A Re-examination of the Halden Reduced-Hours Pilot

*Comment, Journal of Labour and Organisation Studies. K. Varga and T. Holm, Centre for Applied Labour Statistics.*

## Abstract

The Halden pilot reported that 61 organisations maintained output while cutting scheduled hours by 20%, implying a 23.4% gain in output per hour. Using the pilot's microdata, released under the Institute's data-sharing policy, we re-examine the result. Four problems, each documented below, account for most of the reported gain: attrition that was not random, a manager-reported output measure that overstates output relative to organisations' own records, an hours denominator that counts scheduled rather than actual time, and an unadjusted revenue comparison. Correcting the first three, the gain in output per hour falls from 23.4% to 10.8% in the subset of organisations where correction is possible. We then argue that the remaining gain is plausibly a novelty effect, and that the per-hour productivity gains reported for reduced-hours schemes are, in our assessment, entirely an artifact of measurement, selection and novelty.

## 1. Attrition

The working paper states that nine of the 70 enrolled organisations "withdrew during the preparation phase, chiefly for scheduling reasons". The microdata tell a different story. Seven of the nine withdrew after the reduced schedule had begun: four in the first month and three in the second. In exit forms, six of the nine gave workload or inability to maintain output as the main reason, and two gave scheduling. The organisations that found the change hardest were therefore removed from the sample before the outcome was measured. With nine of 70 organisations missing, and those nine plausibly the least successful, the reported sample of 61 is a sample of survivors.

## 2. The output measure

The primary outcome was an index completed by a manager who was also the pilot's internal sponsor. Managers were asked to base the index on organisational records, but were not required to submit them. Twenty-three organisations did submit underlying records (billable hours delivered, tickets closed, units produced, or cases completed). For these 23 we can compare the manager's index with the index implied by the records.

**Table 1. Manager-reported and record-based output, 23 organisations with records**

| Measure | Mean output index (baseline = 100) |
|---|---|
| Manager-reported index | 98.9 |
| Index computed from submitted records | 95.1 |
| Difference | −3.8 points |

In 19 of the 23 organisations the manager-reported index exceeded the record-based index. We do not suggest bad faith. A manager responsible for a change he or she advocated, asked to rate its effect on a scale where 100 means "unchanged", will tend to round toward success. But the difference is systematic, and the headline output figure of 98.7 should not be taken at face value.

## 3. The hours denominator

The pilot computed output per hour by dividing output by the ratio of scheduled hours, 0.8. Twenty-seven organisations used time-tracking software throughout. Their data show average actual weekly hours of 40.3 at baseline and 34.6 during the pilot, a fall of 14.1% rather than 20%. The difference comes from two sources visible in the logs: longer working days on the remaining four days (average +0.7 hours per day), and work logged on the scheduled day off (on average 1.6 hours per week). Some further work on the day off is probably not logged.

Seventeen organisations have both submitted output records and time tracking. In this subset, record-based output was 95.4 and actual hours fell from 40.4 to 34.8 (−13.9%). The implied gain in output per actual hour is 10.8% (95.4 / 86.1), less than half the reported 23.4%.

**Table 2. Implied gain in output per hour under successive corrections**

| Specification | Output | Hours ratio | Gain per hour |
|---|---|---|---|
| As reported (all 61) | 98.7 | 0.800 | +23.4% |
| Record-based output, scheduled hours (23) | 95.1 | 0.800 | +18.9% |
| Manager-reported output, actual hours (27) | 98.4 | 0.859 | +14.6% |
| Record-based output, actual hours (17) | 95.4 | 0.861 | +10.8% |

## 4. Revenue

The working paper reports revenue 1.4% higher than in the previous year. This is a nominal comparison. Consumer prices rose by 4.1% over the same twelve months; in real terms, revenue in participating organisations fell by approximately 2.6%. Revenue is in any case a poor proxy for productivity, but the figure as presented gives a misleading impression of growth.

## 5. Sectoral claims

The pilot concluded that gains in output per hour were "found in every sector" and that the model is "sector-general". This conclusion is an artifact of the per-hour metric. When hours are cut by 20%, any output index above 80 will register as a per-hour gain. Retail and hospitality output fell by 6.9% on the manager-reported measure; the three retail and hospitality organisations among the 23 with records show a fall of 11.2%. A fall in output of this size in a customer-facing business is not evidence that reduced hours work there. The Varden County trial's counter and contact-centre stratum, the only randomised evidence on coverage-bound work, found a fall in output per employee of 11.4% and longer waits for the public. That is, in our view, the most reliable finding in the literature to date.

## 6. Novelty

After the corrections above, a gain in output per actual hour of about 11% remains in the subset of survivors with usable data. We think this residual should not be read as a durable effect. The pilot's own survey shows self-reported energy at work rising by 0.61 standard deviations at month three and falling to 0.29 at month six. Extrapolating this decline, energy would return to baseline at around month ten. A change that staff chose, welcomed and knew to be under evaluation is the classic setting for a novelty effect: effort rises while the change is new and observed, and falls back once it is routine. Six months is not long enough to distinguish a novelty effect from a durable one, and the burden of proof lies with those claiming the latter.

## 7. The meetings hypothesis

The Varden trial's authors report, in an unregistered exploratory analysis, that cuts in recurring meetings correlated with per-hour gains across seven treated offices, and suggest this as a mechanism. We regard this as a post hoc account fitted to a subgroup. A correlation across seven offices, selected for analysis after the results were known, is precisely the kind of finding that does not replicate. The meetings explanation has an intuitive appeal that has outrun its evidence, and it should not be cited as a mechanism.

## 8. Conclusion

Taking the problems together: attrition removed the organisations least able to cope; the output measure overstated output by roughly four points; the hours measure overstated the reduction in time by roughly six points; and the remaining gain coincides with a decaying measure of enthusiasm. We conclude that the per-hour productivity gains reported for reduced-hours schemes are, in our assessment, entirely an artifact of measurement, selection and novelty, and that the best-supported finding is the negative one: where output depends on presence, reduced hours reduce output.

We recommend that future evaluations use record-based output, actual hours, a randomised or at least matched comparison group, follow-up of at least eighteen months, and analysis of all enrolled organisations including those that withdraw.

## Data note

All re-analyses use the Halden pilot microdata (release 1.2). The corrections in Table 2 can only be computed for subsets of organisations, and those subsets were not chosen at random; organisations with time tracking and records may differ from the others. Our corrected estimates therefore describe those subsets, not the pilot as a whole.

response:
# Review: Varga & Holm, "Hours, Output and the Pilot Problem"

The comment does genuinely useful work, and the arithmetic in Tables 1–2 checks out (118.9, 114.6, 110.8; −14.1%, −13.9%; real revenue 1.014 / 1.041 = −2.6%). Its strongest contributions are:

- **The attrition finding.** If the microdata are right, seven of the nine withdrawals happened *after* the schedule began, and six cited workload or output. That contradicts the working paper's description, and the Institute should correct it.
- **The comparison between manager ratings and records.** Managers rated output higher than their own records in 19 of 23 organisations, a systematic gap of 3.8 points.
- **Logged actual hours.** These confirm the scheduled-hours problem with data rather than conjecture.

The problem is that the conclusions go well beyond what these analyses support. In order of importance:

## 1. The conclusion contradicts the paper's own estimate and the Varden trial

After the corrections, the comment's own best estimate is a **+10.8%** gain in output per actual hour. It then concludes that per-hour gains are "entirely an artifact of measurement, selection and novelty."

- Getting from 10.8% to zero rests only on the novelty argument (§2 below), which is the weakest part of the paper.
- The conclusion covers "reduced-hours schemes" generally, but only one pilot is analysed.
- The comment cites the Varden counter stratum as "the most reliable finding in the literature." It does not mention the same trial's **case-processing stratum**: randomised, record-based output, timesheet hours, nine months, and **+12.5% (+6.9 to +18.4)** per actual hour.
- That result was not affected by self-selection, manager ratings or scheduled-hours denominators. Its novelty exposure is also limited: nine months is beyond the point where the comment's own extrapolation puts energy back at baseline.
- Citing Varden where it supports the argument and ignoring it where it does not is a significant weakness for a comment whose stated aim is correcting overclaiming.

A defensible conclusion would be that corrected per-hour gains are about half the reported figure. Whether they persist is unknown. Randomised evidence suggests real gains in non-coverage work and real losses in coverage-bound work.

## 2. The novelty argument is weak

- **The extrapolation.** It uses two survey points (0.61 SD at month 3, 0.29 SD at month 6). A straight line through them reaches zero at about **month 8.7**, not "around month ten." More fundamentally, two points cannot distinguish linear decay from a plateau, and the series may already be levelling off.
- **The wrong variable.** Energy is not output. The comment never shows that *output per hour* declines over time.
- **The direct test was available.** Halden collected the output index monthly, and the authors have the microdata. Plotting output per hour by month, or at least by month 3 versus month 6, for the 17-organisation subset would test the novelty claim directly. Without it, the claim is speculation.
- **"The burden of proof lies with those claiming the latter"** is a rhetorical move, not evidence. It is also a double standard alongside §7, which rejects the meetings hypothesis as post hoc while the novelty account rests on even less.

## 3. Table 2 confounds the corrections with changes in sample

Each row uses a different set of organisations (61, 23, 27, 17). The move from 23.4% to 10.8% therefore mixes two things: the effect of the corrections, and differences between organisations that kept records or used time tracking and those that did not.

- The data note acknowledges this, but the Abstract and Conclusion present 10.8% as *the* corrected figure for the pilot.
- **Fix:** report all four specifications on the same **17-organisation subset**. The manager index with scheduled hours, for these 17 alone, is the right baseline. This isolates the effect of each correction.
- Also state whether means are employee-weighted, as in the original. If they are not, weighting is an additional source of difference.

## 4. The abstract misstates what was done

- It says "Correcting the first three" problems produces 10.8%. But **attrition is not corrected anywhere**: Table 2 adjusts only the output measure and the hours denominator.
- It says four problems "account for most of the reported gain." Revenue has no bearing on the per-hour estimate.

**Attrition can and should be bounded:**
- If the nine withdrawals were similar in size to the remaining organisations and showed *zero* per-hour gain, the mean falls only from about 23.4% to about 20%. A large effect needs either large organisations or substantial output losses among the withdrawals.
- Organisations that left in months 1–2 may have monthly index values for the period before they withdrew. Those values, or a worst-case bounding analysis, would show how much attrition actually matters, instead of leaving it as "plausibly the least successful."

## 5. A numerical inconsistency in §3

The hours decomposition does not add up as written.
- Baseline is 40.3 hours, or about 8.06 hours per day.
- Four days at (8.06 + 0.7) plus 1.6 hours on the day off gives about **36.6 hours**, not the reported 34.6.
- The figures reconcile if the extra time on the remaining days is **+0.7 hours per *week***: 4 × 8.06 + 0.7 + 1.6 ≈ 34.5.

"Per day" looks like an error, but the authors should check.

## 6. §7 misdescribes the Varden meetings analysis

- The seven offices are not "selected for analysis after the results were known." They are the **entire** treated case-processing stratum. The meeting data were collected in month six at managers' request, before the nine-month results.
- The Varden authors already said the analysis cannot establish a mechanism and registered a confirmatory test. The comment criticises a claim they did not make.
- There are legitimate criticisms to make instead:
  - There is no baseline meeting data, so "cuts" cannot actually be measured.
  - The 95% interval on r = 0.71 with n = 7 runs from about −0.1 to 0.95.
- Note too that the 3.3-hour treatment–control difference in meeting time is a randomised comparison, not just a seven-office correlation. That makes it more informative than the comment allows.

## 7. Smaller points

- **Record-based measures are not a clean gold standard.** "Billable hours delivered" partly measures inputs. Tickets closed and units produced differ across organisations and ignore quality. A 3.8-point gap shows managers rate higher than records, not that records are correct. "Overstates output" should be "exceeds record-based output."
- **Retail evidence is thin.** The −11.2% retail figure rests on **three organisations**. Varden's counter stratum is only 5 versus 5 public-sector offices, and its intervals likely need a small-cluster correction. "Most reliable finding in the literature" should be softened accordingly.
- **Inexact quotation.** "Found in every sector" is presented as a quotation, but the working paper says "We find gains in output per hour in every sector represented." Quote it exactly.
- **Deflator.** CPI is a rough deflator for B2B services and non-profit revenue. Sector-specific producer prices would be better. The direction of the correction is surely right, though.
- **Unsupported speculation.** "Some further work on the day off is probably not logged" has no evidence behind it and only pushes in one direction. Either support it or drop it.

## Bottom line

**Keep:** the attrition finding, the records comparison, the actual-hours correction, real revenue, and the per-hour-metric critique of the sectoral claims. Together these support a clear conclusion: the Halden headline roughly doubles the defensible per-hour gain, and the pilot's sector claims fail.

**Revise:**
- Run all corrections on a common subset.
- Bound the attrition effect.
- Test novelty with the monthly output data rather than extrapolating survey energy.
- Engage with Varden's case-processing result.
- Replace "entirely an artifact" with a conclusion matching the authors' own 10.8%.

As written, the comment repeats the error it criticises in the Halden pilot: a headline that goes beyond the evidence.
